book: Still Ruled by Rome: How an Empire Set the Calendar You Live By
intro: Sources and further reading for each chapter. Ancient authors are cited by book and section, so any edition or translation will do. Where a source is free to read online, it is linked. If a link breaks or you spot an error, tell us at hello@sol28.co.uk and we will correct it here.

For the claims in this preface about Kodak, Ethiopia and the International Fixed Calendar, see the notes to Chapters 12 and 15.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: October Means Eight

sources.cite: Censorinus, De Die Natali 20 (AD 238): the early Roman year, its months and its later reform. English translation by W. Maude.
Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.12–1.13: the ten-month year, the months added by Numa, and the month names. Latin text and translation at LacusCurtius.
Denis Feeney, Caesar's Calendar: Ancient Time and the Beginnings of History (University of California Press, 2007).
Ovid, Fasti 1.27–44 and 3.99–166: Romulus' ten-month year beginning in March, and Numa's two added months. Translation by A. S. Kline.
Plutarch, Life of Numa 18–19: Numa adds January and February. LacusCurtius text.
Livy, Periochae 47 (Livius.org translation): the consuls of 153 BC enter office on 1 January.
Suetonius, Life of Augustus 31: Sextilis renamed August. LacusCurtius text.
Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.12.34–35: the Senate's decree renaming Sextilis, quoted in full.
Online Etymology Dictionary, 'October': from Latin octo, eight; the eighth month of the old Roman year.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Year of Confusion

sources.cite: Censorinus, De Die Natali 20.8–11: Caesar's reform and the 445-day year.
Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.14: Caesar's reform, the 'last year of confusion' and the later leap-year error.
Pliny the Elder, Natural History 18.211: Sosigenes and the reform.
Robert Hannah, Greek and Roman Calendars: Constructions of Time in the Classical World (Duckworth, 2005).
Suetonius, Life of Julius Caesar 40: the calendar in disorder through the priests' intercalation, and Caesar's reform. LacusCurtius text.
Plutarch, Life of Caesar 59: the reform, and Cicero's joke that a star would rise 'by decree'. ToposText translation.
Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.14.13–15: the priests' leap-year error and Augustus's correction.
Claus Tøndering, 'The Julian calendar' and 'The Gregorian calendar', Calendar FAQ: the length of the tropical year and the drift of the Julian calendar.
Denis Feeney, Caesar's Calendar (University of California Press, 2007), chapter 6, on the reform and its reception.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Rules of the Roman Year

Censorinus, De Die Natali 20: the 355-day year, odd-numbered months, intercalation and Caesar's ten days.
Varro, On the Latin Language 6.27–6.34: the named days and the day letters.
Livy, History of Rome 9.46: Gnaeus Flavius publishes the calendar.
Codex Justinianus 3.12.2: Constantine's Sunday law of AD 321.
Seneca, On Benefits 1.2 and 7.10: the kalendarium as a moneylender's account book. Suetonius, Life of Augustus 87: 'at the Greek Kalends'.
The Fasti Antiates Maiores, the only surviving pre-Julian calendar (Encyclopaedia Romana, University of Chicago).
William Smith (ed.), A Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities (1875), 'Calendarium'. Useful for its quotations from ancient sources.

Jörg Rüpke, The Roman Calendar from Numa to Constantine (Wiley-Blackwell, 2011); Agnes Kirsopp Michels, The Calendar of the Roman Republic (Princeton University Press, 1967); Denis Feeney, Caesar's Calendar (2007).
Ovid, Fasti, Book 6: the rival claims of Juno and others to June. Translation by A. S. Kline.
Claus Tøndering, Calendar FAQ, 'The Roman calendar': Kalends, Nones and Ides, with worked examples.
